title: US June 2026 Monthly Treasury Deficit
question: What monthly deficit will the U.S. Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service report in the first-print Monthly Treasury Statement for June 2026, Table 1 summary of receipts, outlays, and deficit/surplus, not seasonally adjusted?
resolutionRule: Resolve to the first Monthly Treasury Statement print for June 2026, Table 1 deficit/surplus for the month of June 2026, with deficit positive and surplus negative, converted from the agency's dollars-in-millions presentation to USD billions and rounded to the nearest 1 billion. Ignore later revisions or annual-report restatements.
drivers: June quarterly tax payments usually lift receipts
June 1 payment timing can move outlays across months
tariff receipts are elevated but refund implementation adds uncertainty
interest and entitlement outlays remain high
FY2026 deficit was reported slightly below FY2025 through May after calendar adjustment

reasoning.text: Forecast for the June 2026 Monthly Treasury Statement deficit

reasoning.result: Fetched May 2026 Treasury-reported context: customs duties collected were 22 USD billion, refunds were 22 USD billion, fiscal-year net tariff revenue through May was 189 USD billion versus 81 USD billion a year earlier, and the calendar-adjusted deficit was 2 percent or 24 USD billion below the prior year.

reasoning.call: Checked reporting around June 2025 tariff and fiscal context as a prior-year anchor.
reasoning.result: Fetched June 2025 context reporting Treasury tariff revenue around 27 to 30 USD billion in June 2025, up from 4 USD billion a year earlier, and fiscal-year tariff revenue above 113 USD billion.

reasoning.text: Base-rate step: the most relevant reference class is recent June MTS prints because June contains quarterly estimated tax payments and has strong seasonality. The recent June deficits of 27, 66, and 228 billion imply a wide but positive-deficit center; the two most recent years point closer to 50 billion than to the 2023 outlier.

I start with a recent-June base of about (27 + 66) / 2 = 46.5 billion, add roughly 20 billion for higher interest and entitlement outlays, add 10 billion for tariff-refund and policy noise, and round to a 72 billion point. The 80% interval is set wide at -35 to 210 billion to cover a possible June surplus from strong receipts and a 2023-like high-deficit outlier if payment timing or refunds raise outlays.

Counter-consideration: elevated tariff receipts and June tax collections could produce a small surplus, especially if refunds are not concentrated in June, which is why the lower bound is negative despite the point being a deficit.
